extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of medieval Italian history
extracted.subtask_description: A historical narrative recounting political, military, and social events in Cremona and neighbouring Lombard cities (c.1200–1320), with commentary on faction, governance, treaties, and civic ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difunion of the citizens is the worst evil in a city
rubrics_metrics.description: “Difunion of the citizens is, indeed, according to him, the worst evil in a city; for what mortal pestilence can bring upon them greater damage than discord?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Camp0 elaborates that discord not only precipitates families to ruin but “exterminates powerful and famous cities,” tearing up principalities and kingdoms; examples and rhetorical metaphors (e.g., Cyrus dividing the Euphrates) are used to show the practical consequences of civic division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union (concord) sustains and increases the commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: “All things are maintained and increased by concord; and go to ruin by disunion; union brings victory, and discord defeat.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats concord as the positive normative standard for civic health: united citizens can resist enemies and preserve strength and beauty; supporting examples include military resilience and rhetorical analogies to united water versus divided rivulets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oaths and treaties have limited reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: “But of what avail are oaths and treaties, which the nature of man and the form of the government will not permit to be observed?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Camp0 warns that formal promises often fail when human nature or institutional arrangements make observance impracticable; this is offered as a caution about relying solely on written agreements to secure lasting peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sole reliance on sermons and exhortations cannot secure republican unity
rubrics_metrics.description: “How long will republicans be the dupes of their own simplicity! how long will they depend upon sermons, prayers, orations, declamations, in honour of brotherly love, and against discords, when they know that, without human means, it is but tempting and insulting Providence...?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Camp0 argues that moral suasion is insufficient; effective preservation of liberty and social order requires concrete human measures (institutional balance and force), not merely exhortation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factions (e.g., Guelphs and Ghibellines) are politically pernicious
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the year 1242 began to take root in Cremona those abominable and pernicious factions of Guelphs and Ghibellines... occasioned an infinite expense of the blood of the citizens, an inestimable destruction of wealth, an unspeakable perdition of families, and a most melancholy and miserable ruin of the country.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage uses the concrete historical example of the Guelph–Ghibelline split to illustrate the catastrophic social, economic, and demographic costs of factionalism; it functions as a negative criterion for evaluating civic political arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peace terms often required reciprocal expulsion of exiles
rubrics_metrics.description: In negotiated peaces recorded here, a principal condition was that “all the cities should expel each other's exiles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative records this recurring diplomatic/procedural term as a standard mechanism intended to stabilize inter-city relations, with the implication that such terms aimed to remove internal spoilers but also produced further displacements and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary magistracies (consuls, podestà) as mechanisms to manage civil discord
rubrics_metrics.description: The cities repeatedly appointed consuls for fixed short terms (e.g., six months) or podestàs as means to address internal contention and to administer justice and military leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text documents the recurring use of externally or locally appointed magistrates (podestà, consuls, captains) and time-limited offices to attempt to stabilize factional tensions; it portrays these institutions as customary remedies though not always successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leagues and collective military hiring as common defensive/political response
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities formed confederations, sent ambassadors, and agreed to hire troops “at the common expense, and for the common defence, a thousand horse and a thousand foot,” or entered into leagues under captains-general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Camp0 describes interstate alliances and pooled military forces as standard practice for confronting threats or enforcing political goals; these are presented as expected tools of city-state diplomacy and warfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers may prohibit mass popular penitential movements if they threaten political stability
rubrics_metrics.description: When pilgrimages and penitential movements arose aiming to restore peace among parties, Pallavicino “prohibited, under severe penalties, these kind of pilgrimages in Cremona and Brescia, because he feared they would prove the ruin of those seditions and divisions by which he maintained the domination of those cities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This episode is recorded as an example of a ruler taking repressive measures against popular religious-political mobilization when it is perceived to endanger the existing power structure; it illustrates a governance principle balancing public order against civil liberties.
